Section 9.2 splits the variability in a regression response into the piece
**explained by the model** and the piece **left in the errors**:
$$SSTotal = SSModel + SSE,$$
with $SSModel = \sum(\hat y - \bar y)^2$, $SSE = \sum(y - \hat y)^2$ and
$SSTotal = \sum(y-\bar y)^2$. Dividing by degrees of freedom (1 for the
model, $n-2$ for the error) gives mean squares, and their ratio is the
**F-statistic** $F = MSModel/MSE$, compared to an $F_{1,\,n-2}$ upper tail
to test $H_0\colon\beta_1 = 0$ (model ineffective). For a single predictor
this F-test is **always equivalent to the two-tail t-test for the slope**
(though $F = t^2$), and $R^2 = SSModel/SSTotal$ is the percent of response
variability the model explains. Two extra quantities: the standard
deviation of the error $s_\epsilon = \sqrt{MSE}$, and the standard error of
the slope $SE = s_\epsilon / (s_x\sqrt{n-1})$. As usual we verify the
parametric answers with **randomization** (permutation F-tests, 10000
shuffles, seed 2026). Exercises are from *Statistics: Unlocking the Power
of Data* (Lock⁵, 3rd ed., pp. 640–644): Skill Builders 9.34–9.45 dissect
and rebuild ANOVA tables; applied exercises 9.46–9.63 cover Facebook
friends and brain structure, cereal calories, printer prices, Verbal SAT
and GPA, football and cognition, water striders, arm spans, hockey points
and penalty minutes, exercise vs TV, country health expenditure, California
home sales, and a free-choice exploration.

```{python}
#| include: false
import os
from pathlib import Path
_root = Path.cwd()
while not (_root / "_quarto.yml").exists():
    _root = _root.parent
os.chdir(_root)
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt, seaborn as sns
from scipy import stats
sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")

def anova_reg(ss_model, sse, n, name="Model"):
    """Build a full one-predictor regression ANOVA table from pieces."""
    ss_total = ss_model + sse
    mse = sse / (n - 2)
    F = ss_model / mse
    p = stats.f.sf(F, 1, n - 2)
    tab = pd.DataFrame({
        "Source": ["Model", "Error", "Total"],
        "df": [1, n - 2, n - 1],
        "SS": [round(ss_model, 3), round(sse, 3), round(ss_total, 3)],
        "MS": [round(ss_model, 3), round(mse, 3), ""],
        "F": [round(F, 3), "", ""],
        "p-value": [float(f"{p:.3g}") if p < 1e-4 else round(float(p), 4),
                    "", ""]}).set_index("Source")
    return tab

def reg_pieces(x, y):
    """Return (SSModel, SSE, SSTotal, n) for a least squares fit."""
    x = np.asarray(x, float); y = np.asarray(y, float)
    res = stats.linregress(x, y)
    fit = res.intercept + res.slope * x
    sse = ((y - fit) ** 2).sum()
    sst = ((y - y.mean()) ** 2).sum()
    return sst - sse, sse, sst, len(x)

def perm_F(x, y, reps=10000, seed=2026):
    """Randomization F-test for a simple linear model."""
    x = np.asarray(x, float); y = np.asarray(y, float)
    ssm, sse, sst, n = reg_pieces(x, y)
    Fobs = (ssm / 1) / (sse / (n - 2))
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    Fs = np.empty(reps)
    for i in range(reps):
        ys = r.permutation(y)
        s, e, t_, n_ = reg_pieces(x, ys)
        Fs[i] = (s / 1) / (e / (n_ - 2))
    return Fs, Fobs, float((Fs >= Fobs).mean())

def sim_hist(sims, stat, xlabel="Simulated F-statistics", bins=40,
             figsize=(6, 3)):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=figsize)
    sns.histplot(x=sims, bins=bins, ax=ax, color="#4c72b0")
    mask = sims >= stat
    if mask.any():
        sns.histplot(x=sims[mask], bins=bins, ax=ax, color="#c44e52")
    ax.axvline(stat, color="black", lw=1.5)
    ax.set_xlabel(xlabel); ax.set_ylabel("Simulated statistics")
    plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

def reg_fit(x, y):
    x = np.asarray(x, float); y = np.asarray(y, float)
    res = stats.linregress(x, y)
    n = len(x)
    fit = res.intercept + res.slope * x
    se_e = np.sqrt(((y - fit) ** 2).sum() / (n - 2))
    t = res.slope / res.stderr
    p = 2 * stats.t.sf(abs(t), n - 2)
    return pd.Series({
        "n": n, "intercept": round(res.intercept, 4),
        "slope": round(res.slope, 4), "SE(slope)": round(res.stderr, 4),
        "t": round(t, 3), "p-value": float(f"{p:.3g}"),
        "r": round(res.rvalue, 4), "R2": round(res.rvalue ** 2, 4),
        "s_e": round(se_e, 4)})
```

::: {.panel-tabset}


## Exercise 9.48

Predicting Prices of Printers: $Price = 378 - 18.6\,\text{CostColor}$,
ANOVA: Regression SS = 57604, Error SS = 78633 (df 18), F = 13.19, P = 0.002.

**(a)** Predicted price at CostColor = 10: $378 - 18.6(10) = \mathbf{\$192}$.

**(b)** The slope is **negative** (−18.6): cheaper printers tend to **cost
more** per page for color printing.

**(c)** $n = df_{Total} + 1 = 19 + 1 = \mathbf{20}$ printers.

**(d)** $R^2 = 57604/136237 = \mathbf{42.3\%}$: color printing cost explains
about 42.3% of the variability in printer price.

**(e)** **F = 13.19, p-value = 0.002 < 0.05**: yes, the linear model is
effective at predicting price from color printing cost.

## Exercise 9.50

Football and Cognition: $r = -0.366$ (p = 0.015), $t = -2.55$, ANOVA
F = 6.50 (df 1, 42), all p = 0.015.

**(a)** $r = \mathbf{-0.366}$, **p-value = 0.015**.

**(b)** Slope = **−3.34**: each additional year of football is associated
with 3.34 points lower cognitive score, on average. $t = -3.34/1.31 =
\mathbf{-2.55}$, **p-value = 0.015**.

**(c)** **F = 6.50**, **p-value = 0.015**.

**(d)** The **three p-values are identical (0.015)** — for one predictor,
the correlation test, slope t-test and ANOVA F-test are all equivalent
(note $F = (-2.55)^2 \approx 6.50$).

**(e)** At a 5% level, all three tests reject $H_0$: there is significant
evidence that more years playing football are associated with lower
cognitive scores (an observational association, not proof of causation).

## Exercise 9.53

How Big Is an Arm Span? (PASeniors): compare Armspan ~ Height vs
Armspan ~ Foot.

```{python}
#| include: false
pa = pd.read_csv("data/ch09/PASeniors.csv")
fit_h = reg_fit(pa.Height, pa.Armspan)
fit_f = reg_fit(pa.Foot, pa.Armspan)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
pd.DataFrame({"Armspan ~ Height": fit_h,
              "Armspan ~ Foot": fit_f}).to_string()
```

```{python}
#| include: false
_, Fh, ph = perm_F(pa.Height, pa.Armspan)
_, Ff, pf = perm_F(pa.Foot, pa.Armspan)
```

**(a)** Slope: Height **0.91** vs Foot **3.48** — **Foot has the larger
slope** (but different units, so not directly comparable).

**(b)** Standard deviation of the error: Height **9.41 cm** vs Foot
**9.94 cm** — **Height has the smaller** $s_\epsilon$.

**(c)** R²: Height **51.5%** vs Foot **46.0%** — **Height explains more**
variability (randomization F-tests confirm both models are effective,
p ≈ `{python} f"{ph:.4f}"` and p ≈ `{python} f"{pf:.4f}"`).

**(d)** **Height** is the more effective predictor of arm span: smaller
error sd and larger R².

## Exercise 9.55

More Computation on Points and Penalty Minutes: verify $s_\epsilon$ and SE
using Table 9.3 ($s_x = 24.92$, $n = 26$).

```{python}
#| echo: false
se_e = np.sqrt(8607.7 / 24)
SE = se_e / (24.92 * np.sqrt(25))
pd.Series({"s_e = sqrt(8607.7/24)": round(se_e, 3),
           "SE = s_e/(s_x*sqrt(n-1))": round(SE, 4)}).to_string()
```

**(a)** $s_\epsilon = \sqrt{SSE/(n-2)} = \sqrt{8607.7/24} =
\mathbf{18.94}$ — matches S = 18.938 in the output.

**(b)** $SE = 18.94/(24.92\sqrt{25}) = \mathbf{0.152}$ — matches the output
SE for the PenMins coefficient.

## Exercise 9.59

Time Spent Exercising or Watching TV? (ExerciseHours, n = 50): predict
Exercise from TV, three equivalent tests.

```{python}
#| include: false
exh = pd.read_csv("data/ch09/ExerciseHours.csv")
fitTV = reg_fit(exh.TV, exh.Exercise)
sSm, sSe, sSt, n = reg_pieces(exh.TV, exh.Exercise)
F = (sSm / 1) / (sSe / (n - 2))
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
fitTV.to_string()
pd.Series({"F = MSModel/MSE": round(F, 3),
           "ANOVA p-value": float(f"{stats.f.sf(F, 1, 48):.3g}"),
           "F (= t^2)": round(fitTV['t'] ** 2, 3)}).to_string()
```

```{python}
#| include: false
Fs, Fobs, p_perm = perm_F(exh.TV, exh.Exercise)
```

**(a)** t-test for the TV coefficient: $t = \mathbf{2.04}$, df = 48,
**p-value = 0.047**.

**(b)** ANOVA: **F = 4.15** (df 1, 48), **p-value = 0.047**.

**(c)** t-test for the correlation: $r = \mathbf{0.282}$, and the
correlation t-statistic is the same **2.04** with the same p-value 0.047.

**(d)** All three tests give **identical statistics and p-values** ($F =
t^2$); all reject $H_0$ at 5% (barely) — significant evidence that TV hours
help predict exercise hours, with randomization agreement (p ≈
`{python} f"{p_perm:.4f}"`).

## Exercise 9.62

Which Variable Is Best in Homes for Sale in California? Predict Size;
SSTotal = 6,563,872 sq ft².

```{python}
#| include: false
sst_size = ((homes.Size - homes.Size.mean()) ** 2).sum()
rows = []
for pred in ["Price", "Beds", "Baths"]:
    ssm, sse, sst, n_ = reg_pieces(homes[pred], homes.Size)
    res = stats.linregress(homes[pred], homes.Size)
    t = res.slope / res.stderr
    rows.append({"Predictor": pred,
                 "SSModel": round(ssm),
                 "% of SSTotal": round(100 * ssm / sst, 1),
                 "F": round((ssm / 1) / (sse / 28), 3),
                 "p-value": float(f"{2 * stats.t.sf(abs(t), 28):.3g}")})
best = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("Predictor")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
pd.Series({"SSTotal (Size)": round(sst_size)}).to_string()
best.to_string()
```

**(a)** Total variability: $SSTotal = \mathbf{6{,}563{,}872}$ (same for any
predictor — it does not use X).

**(b)** **Baths** explains the most (largest SSModel): **41.3%** of the
variability in home sizes.

**(c)** $SSModel_{Baths} = \mathbf{2{,}709{,}896}$ sq ft² = **41.3%** of
SSTotal.

**(d)** The weakest predictor is **Beds**: only **20.2%** (SSModel =
1,323,367).

**(e)** **Yes — still effective:** the ANOVA F-test for Beds gives
p-value = 0.013 < 0.05, so even the weakest variable explains a
statistically significant share of the variability.

## Exercise 9.63

Explore a Relationship between Two Quantitative Variables: we choose
**Cereal**, response = Calories, explanatory = Fat (neither pairing is
analyzed elsewhere in Chapter 9).

**(a)** Dataset Cereal (n = 30 cereals); response: Calories; explanatory:
Fat (grams per cup).

**(b)** Scatterplot and conditions:

```{python}
#| include: false
cer = pd.read_csv("data/ch09/Cereal.csv")
fitFat = reg_fit(cer.Fat, cer.Calories)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 3.4))
ax.scatter(cer.Fat, cer.Calories, color="#4c72b0", alpha=0.75)
xs = np.linspace(cer.Fat.min(), cer.Fat.max(), 50)
ax.plot(xs, fitFat["intercept"] + fitFat["slope"] * xs, color="#c44e52", lw=2)
ax.set_xlabel("Fat (g)"); ax.set_ylabel("Calories")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

A roughly linear positive band, fairly even scatter — conditions
reasonably met.

**(c)–(g)** All three inference routes, plus a randomization check:

```{python}
#| include: false
sSm, sSe, sSt, n = reg_pieces(cer.Fat, cer.Calories)
Fc = (sSm / 1) / (sSe / (n - 2))
_, _, p_permC = perm_F(cer.Fat, cer.Calories)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
fitFat.to_string()
pd.Series({"r": fitFat["r"],
           "correlation p-value": fitFat["p-value"],
           "F-statistic": round(Fc, 3),
           "F (= t^2)": round(fitFat["t"] ** 2, 3),
           "randomization p-value": round(p_permC, 4)}).to_string()
```

**(c)** $r = \mathbf{0.681}$, p-value $\approx 0.00004$.

**(d)** $\widehat{Calories} = 106.1 + 21.6\,\text{Fat}$; t = 4.91,
p-value $\approx 0.00004$.

**(e)** **F = 24.13** (df 1, 28), p-value $\approx 0.00004$.

**(f)** **R² = 46.3%**: fat content explains about 46% of the variability
in calories.

**(g)** The model is clearly effective (all three equivalent tests agree,
and the randomization F-test concurs, p ≈ `{python} f"{p_permC:.4f}"`),
with fat the strongest single nutrient predictor of calories in these
cereals — though over half the variability remains unexplained.
